# Speedle AI — AI agent authorization and access control

> Speedle is an open-source (UPL-1.0) authorization engine with the SPDL policy language. It consists of ADS (decisions) and PMS (policy management), SDKs in six languages, Speedle Cloud (hosted), and Speedle AI (authorization for and with AI agents, an MCP server, and the policy-modeler skill).

Source: https://ai.speedle.io/
Chinese: https://ai.speedle.io/zh/

Speedle AI — AI for access control, access control for AI — applies the engine to authorization for AI agents: MCP tool calls, permission-aware RAG, agent-to-agent (A2A) calls, zero standing privileges (ZSP) and the AI lifecycle from training data to model release. Everything here is a solution pattern on the Speedle policy engine; none of it is a shipped integration with an ML or agent platform.

## What Speedle is

Speedle is an open-source authorization engine, written in Go, for externalizing fine-grained access-control decisions. It evaluates RBAC and ABAC policies and keeps authorization logic outside application code. It is licensed under the Universal Permissive License (UPL) 1.0.

- **PMS (Policy Management Service):** the policy administration point; stores and serves policies.
- **ADS (Authorization Decision Service):** the policy decision point; answers `isAllowed` requests.
- **SPDL (Speedle Policy Definition Language):** the human-readable policy language.
- **SDKs in six languages:** Python, Java, Go, C#/.NET, Rust and Node.js/TypeScript.
- **Speedle Cloud:** hosted authorization for developers; sign-in on cloud.speedle.io opens soon.
- **Speedle AI:** authorization for and with AI agents, the planned Speedle MCP server and the speedle-policy-modeler skill.

Links: [documentation](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/), [SPDL reference](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/), [getting started](https://engine.speedle.io/quick-start/), [SDKs](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/sdks/), [Playground](https://engine.speedle.io/playground/), [Speedle Cloud docs](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/cloud/).

### Current SDK versions

All published SDKs are at 0.2.0: `speedle` on PyPI, `io.speedle:speedle-sdk` on Maven Central, `github.com/teramoby/speedle-sdk/go` for Go, `Speedle.Sdk` on NuGet and `speedle` on crates.io. The npm packages `@speedle/sdk` and `@speedle/mcp` are not published yet.

## SPDL in brief

The full grammar, every built-in function and the complete syntax are in the [SPDL reference](https://engine.speedle.io/docs/spdl/). This section summarizes what the AI patterns use.

A policy is an effect, a subject, one or more actions, a resource and an optional condition. A role policy assigns a role or grants a role an action:

```
POLICY     = (grant | deny) SUBJECT ACTION RESOURCE [if CONDITION]
ROLEPOLICY = (grant | deny) SUBJECT ROLE [on RESOURCE] [if CONDITION]
```

- **Effect:** `grant` allows; `deny` overrides every grant. A request with no applicable grant is denied (default deny).
- **Subject:** one or more principals of type `user`, `group`, `entity` or `role`, optionally with `from IDD` to name an identity domain. An AND group `(principal, principal)` requires every listed principal; separate groups are alternatives.
- **Actions and resources:** comma-separated action names and one resource, where the `expr:` prefix introduces a Go regular expression.
- **Role policies:** assigning a role alone does not create permissions; a policy must grant the role an action. `grant role manager employee` makes the manager role inherit the employee role.
- **Conditions:** boolean expressions over attributes, constants, operators and functions. Types are string, numeric, bool, datetime and arrays; operators include `==`, `!=`, `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=`, `=~`, `in`, `&&`, `||` and `!`.
- **Attributes:** ADS provides built-ins such as `request_user`, `request_groups`, `request_entity`, `request_resource`, `request_action`, `request_time`, `request_year`, `request_month`, `request_day`, `request_hour` and `request_weekday`. The PEP supplies customer attributes such as tenant, clearance, amount or token claims.
- **Functions:** built-ins `Sqrt`, `Max`, `Min`, `Sum`, `Avg` and `IsSubSet`; custom functions call an external REST endpoint on self-hosted Speedle. Speedle Cloud does not run custom functions.

Examples:

```spdl
# Role inheritance: a manager also holds the employee role
grant role manager employee

# Deny over grant: employees may read docs, but not the finance subtree
grant role employee read,list expr:^/docs/
deny role employee read expr:^/docs/finance

# An AND group: both roles are required
grant (role designer, role dba) update db_design_doc

# A condition over a customer attribute and a built-in
grant role analyst read expr:^/reports/ if region == user_region && request_time < deadline
```

By design: a condition on an attribute missing from the request does not match, because the policy enforcement point (PEP) must supply every attribute a policy references. Attributes supplied by the PEP also take priority over built-ins such as `request_time`, `request_user` and `request_resource`.

## Speedle AI

Speedle AI has two connected directions:

- **Use AI to manage access:** AI helping people design, manage and check access policies with the open-source policy modeler skill, the planned Speedle MCP server and an AI-based risk-detection approach being built.
- **Control what AI can access:** policy patterns that govern what AI systems and agents may do while they are built and while they run.

Both rest on enforceable policy decisions. Speedle decides; the application enforces the decision. The home page gives one sentence and one representative SPDL rule per area; the full examples are on the patterns page.

## Use AI to manage access

### Speedle policy modeler skill

An open-source Agent Skill at `skills/speedle-policy-modeler/` in teramoby/ai.speedle.io, for any agent that supports the Agent Skills format. It reads a company regulation, employee handbook or access matrix; asks the document owner to clarify missing org structure, roles, resources, attributes, exceptions and approval chains in small prioritized batches; and writes an RBAC + ABAC model.

Outputs: `policies.spdl` in the Speedle file-store format, a `model.md` design document with a Mermaid role-inheritance diagram and a rationale for every policy, a `test-cases.json` suite, `results.md`, and `clarifications.md`. The skill refuses to guess an authorization rule; every policy cites a handbook clause or a confirmed answer.

Example runs: English and Chinese synthetic handbooks. Both pass `spctl check` and all 37 authorization cases against a local PMS and ADS. The SPDL uses exact or prefix resource expressions only, so the evaluator uses hash-map and radix-tree lookups.

The `SKILL.md` frontmatter follows the Agent Skills format with `name` and `description`. For a generic install, copy the skill folder into your agent's skills directory, then ask the agent to model `./employee-handbook.md`.

- Claude Code example: copy `skills/speedle-policy-modeler/` to `~/.claude/skills/` for a personal skill or `.claude/skills/` for a project skill, then run `/speedle-policy-modeler ./employee-handbook.md`.
- Codex CLI or IDE example: copy `skills/speedle-policy-modeler/` to `~/.agents/skills/`, then type `$speedle-policy-modeler ./employee-handbook.md` to mention the skill and provide the handbook.

- Skill folder: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler
- English sample: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/blob/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler/examples/en/model.md
- Chinese sample: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/blob/main/skills/speedle-policy-modeler/examples/zh/model.md
- OpenAI Build skills documentation: https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/build-skills — lists `$HOME/.agents/skills` as the personal Codex skill directory and `$` as explicit skill invocation in Codex CLI or the IDE extension.

### Speedle MCP (launch preview)

`@speedle/mcp` is planned as one npm package with a `speedle-mcp` binary that runs as a local stdio MCP server for authorization work, with two deliberately separate modes. It is not published on npm yet.

- **check mode:** registers only `is_allowed` by default and reads only ADS configuration. `diagnose`, `all_granted_roles` and `all_granted_permissions` are opt-in through the `--expose-diagnose`, `--expose-all-granted-roles` and `--expose-all-granted-permissions` flags. `diagnose` works only with self-hosted Speedle; the server will not start with it against Speedle Cloud. It answers authorization questions through the Speedle ADS REST API using subject, resource, action and typed attributes; it does not enforce anything in the calling application.
- **manage mode:** registers only the management tools and reads only PMS configuration for designing and managing Speedle policies through the PMS REST API: services, authorization policies, role policies, SPDL validation and effective-policy explanation helpers. A read-only option exists and destructive deletes require explicit target confirmation.

Security rule: never give the manage mode to an agent that is itself governed by these policies. An agent holding both check and management tools could be prompted into granting itself access. Give a governed agent `is_allowed` only, which is the check-mode default: `diagnose`, `all_granted_roles` and `all_granted_permissions` show policies, conditions and grants, so turn them on only in a check server for policy authors and operators, and never pass the `--expose-*` flags to the agent's server. There is no default mode that exposes both; running with no mode is planned to print usage and exit non-zero.

Install and MCP client configuration snippets on the site are future launch examples, marked "Available at launch". They do not work today.

### AI-based risk detection (being built)

AI-based risk detection is a direction Speedle is exploring and building, not a shipped feature. The approach looks across more dimensions and relationships than a single rule, for example unusual combinations of agent, user, data and task context.

Policy keeps the veto. The target flow is: request context, then the deterministic policy decision, then AI risk signals, then a final decision. A policy deny stops at the decision step; risk signals can add scrutiny or protection but can never turn a policy deny into an allow. The target flow is at https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#risk-detection

## Control what AI can access

Speedle's policy engine applied wherever AI systems touch data, models, tools and other agents. Each area has an enforcement point in the application; it asks Speedle before it acts and enforces the answer. Identity comes in from the IdP; decisions and explanations go out to the audit trail. The SPDL examples are solution patterns, not shipped platform integrations. The home page summarizes each area with one sentence and one representative rule; the full examples are on https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/.

### Build: data and training

Training jobs read datasets, use compute and write checkpoints. The application asks before each dataset read, job start and checkpoint export, passing sensitivity, tenant, consent and region as attributes.

- Subjects: training pipelines as entities; ML engineers and their teams.
- Resources and actions: datasets `read`, training jobs `start`, checkpoints `export`.
- Enforcement point: the data loader before it opens a dataset, the job scheduler before it allocates compute, and the artifact store before an export.
- SPDL example rules: consent and region checked per dataset, restricted data denied outright, and a GPU-hour limit on job start.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-data

### Build: model release

Registering, approving, promoting and rolling back models are separate actions with separate owners. Separation of duties keeps the person who trained a model from approving it.

- Subjects: ML engineers, release managers and the service identities of release pipelines.
- Resources and actions: models and endpoints with `register`, `approve`, `promote` and `rollback`.
- Enforcement point: the model registry and the release pipeline, before each change of model or endpoint state.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-release

### Run: inference and permission-aware RAG

Users, apps and tenants call models. For permission-aware RAG (retrieval-augmented generation), the retriever asks Speedle about each document or collection before its content enters the prompt, so the model only sees what the person behind the request may read.

- Subjects: the user behind the request with their groups; client applications and tenants as entities.
- Resources and actions: collections and documents `retrieve`; models `invoke`.
- Enforcement point: the retriever before a document enters the prompt, and the API gateway or inference service before it routes a request.
- SPDL example rules: a document is retrieved only inside the user's tenant and at a label the user is cleared for; legal-hold documents are denied; apps call only the model tiers in their plan.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-rag

### Run: agents acting for users

The agent has its own identity, and the user's delegation is proven by a signed delegation token, not by claims in the request. The enforcement point verifies the token, then asks Speedle twice and allows only if both checks pass: the agent within the token's scope, and the delegating user with their own permissions now. If the user loses a permission after the token was issued, the agent loses it at the next request. A refund above 100 also needs a recorded human approval by someone other than the user.

1. Verify the token: signature, issuer, expiry, and that it was issued to this agent.
2. Agent scope: ask Speedle with the agent as subject and the token's scope as attributes.
3. Delegator now: ask Speedle with the delegating user, named by the token's `sub` claim, as subject.

- Subjects: the agent as an entity for the scope check; the delegating user, taken from the verified token, for the second check.
- Resources and actions: tickets `read` and `update`; orders `refund`, with the amount as an attribute. All limited to the actions and resources in the token's scope.
- Enforcement point: the agent runtime or the application backend before the action reaches the business system. It verifies the token and passes only verified claims to Speedle.
- Human approval: the enforcement point verifies the signed approval record for the refund and passes its approver as `approved_by` in the second check. The approver must not be the user.
- Self-hosted option: one check, with the token and the delegator evaluated by the custom functions `DelegationValid` and `DelegatorAllowed`. Speedle Cloud does not run custom functions.
- SPDL example rules: the agent gets its role in three steps (token not expired, action listed, resource listed), so it holds only within the token's scope; the delegator's grants ask about the user alone, so revoking the user's role denies the agent at the next request; a refund above 100 is granted only with an approver other than the user.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-agents

A runnable local sample of both patterns, with a demo token issuer, the enforcement point and the custom-function server, is in the repository: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/samples/delegation

### Run: tool calls over MCP

Every tool call is checked before it runs. The tool is the resource, the call is the action, and the arguments become attributes, so limits such as a refund amount are part of the policy.

- Subjects: agents, each with its own entity identity and role, so privileges stay per agent and per tool.
- Resources and actions: tools `call`, with the tool arguments as attributes.
- Enforcement point: the MCP client host, or a gateway in front of MCP servers, before the tool executes.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-mcp

### Run: agent-to-agent (A2A) authorization

Each hop in a delegation chain is checked. The callee may receive only scopes the caller already holds, and the chain has a hop limit, so delegation only narrows permissions.

- Subjects: calling agents, identified as entities.
- Resources and actions: other agents and their skills `call`, with the requested scopes, the caller's scopes and the hop count as attributes.
- Enforcement point: the calling agent before it sends a task, or the receiving agent before it accepts one.
- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#lc-a2a

### Run: zero standing privileges (ZSP)

Just-in-time, short-lived, narrowly scoped credentials can support a zero standing privileges (ZSP) pattern when token issuance and other controls are in place. Speedle is where you define your ZSP strategy as policy and enforce it on every request: access exists only within the time window and conditions you write in SPDL. On self-hosted Speedle Engine, the policy checks a positive and short lifetime, that the token is not issued or valid in the future beyond a 60-second clock-skew allowance, that it has not expired, and, through a read-only custom function, that it is unused in the issuer's store. (Speedle Cloud does not support custom external functions.) The application or enforcement layer then consumes a single-use token atomically before the operation; production also needs a trusted component that verifies the token and binds its claims to the subject, resource, action and task scope before its claims reach the policy.

- Full example: https://ai.speedle.io/patterns/#zsp

A runnable local sample with PMS, ADS and the custom function, including the atomic consume step, is in the repository: https://github.com/teramoby/ai.speedle.io/tree/main/samples/zsp

### Cross-cutting concerns

- **Identity integration:** Speedle is the authorization decision point. Authentication comes from the IdP or OAuth authorization server, for users and for agents; MCP authorization builds on OAuth. The application maps verified identities to principals and Speedle decides on the principals it is given.
- **Audit and explainability:** Speedle's diagnose API returns the decision, the reason, the effective roles and the policies examined, including which one matched and why. Applications log each decision with the agent and the delegating human. Diagnose exposes policy and request details, so keep it to trusted operators.
- **Risk mapping:** the patterns map to OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency: an agent with more functionality, permission or autonomy than its task needs. Per-agent roles, per-tool checks, task- and time-bound delegation and human approval for high-risk actions narrow each of the three.
- **Boundary:** Speedle does not detect prompt injection, filter model input or output, or verify model and dataset supply chains; use dedicated controls for those. It bounds what a compromised or misled agent can do: Speedle answers deny to any request outside policy, whatever the prompt said.
